title: Returning from Venice, learning dance bands, Indianapolis, then New Orleans
summary: War threatens, so he returns to Chicago, learns dance-band playing at weddings and a Decatur hotel job, spends nine years with the Indianapolis Symphony, then takes the New Orleans Symphony job under Massimo Freccia.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: How did you have to come back to the States?

Well, I was going to school, studying in Venice. And I had about two more years to go and get a degree. And the war broke out. And I was an American citizen and all American citizens were urged to return to the States on account of the imminent pressing state of affairs. You know, Hitler was invading all over and it looked like there was going to be a war. So that's how I came back. And I've been here ever since. What did you come to when you first got back? Well, when I first came back, I wound up in Chicago. That's where the folks lived then, you know. And I stayed in Chicago about a year and I just played in Grand Park summer concerts. And I also got acquainted with playing in a dance band too. I didn't know a thing about playing in a dance band. Having come from school in Italy, you know. So I learned by playing Saturday night jobs here and there. First in Polish weddings or Italian weddings in Chicago. Little by little I learned how to play a beat, you know. You just don't play a dance beat just like that. You gotta learn it. So I picked that up and actually I hadn't been in Chicago, let's see, a few months. I got a job in Decatur, Illinois in a hotel, you know. And this thing lasted a whole summer. And this was a combination, dinner band and dance band. And I really learned a lot from that. Got so, I got a real swinging beat, you know. And I got so good at it, the band, in fact the whole band got so good, they were asked to stay. But I had already written a contract to go to Indianapolis with the Indianapolis Symphony. So I had to leave and that was, by the way, my first year with the Indianapolis Symphony. Which was the last about nine years engagement. And then what did you do after you left Indianapolis? Well, actually, this last year I hadn't signed up for the coming year. Yeah, I hadn't signed up a contract. And I was in New York and I was in the union there, a musician's union. And I met this Italian man and he said, oh, you play bass? He says, you're Italian. He was impressed by the fact that I spoke Italian. He says, I got a good job for you. He says, I, we got a fine orchestra in New Orleans, a symphony. He says, an Italian conductor, his name is Massimo Freccia. He says, you, you come down there, you'll be happy. It's warm all the time. He says, well, actually, I was, I really wanted to make a change anyway. So it didn't take very much to persuade me. I mean, I, I signed up right there and then, and that's how it happened. It comes to New Orleans. And that was, I came, the first year that Massimo Freccia started conducting the New Orleans Symphony.
